claims.text: Thermal annealing of as-received Q235 steel alters its grain-boundary character.
Thermal annealing of Q235 steel promotes pre-oxide formation.
Annealing-induced grain-boundary changes promote oxide nucleation during high-temperature salt exposure.
Grain boundaries in Q235 steel act as preferential sites for oxide nucleation.
Annealed Q235 steel develops a more continuous oxide scale under salt exposure at 700–900 °C than untreated Q235 steel.
The high-temperature oxide scale on annealed Q235 steel is more adherent than that on untreated Q235 steel.
The high-temperature oxide scale on annealed Q235 steel is chemically enriched in beneficial elements such as Cr or Mn.
Annealed Q235 steel forms a denser oxide scale at high temperature than untreated Q235 steel.
The oxide scale formed on annealed Q235 steel is more chemically stable at high temperature than the scale on untreated Q235 steel.
A continuous, enriched oxide scale limits corrosive-ion ingress into Q235 steel.
Limiting corrosive-ion ingress reduces high-temperature corrosion degradation of annealed Q235 steel relative to untreated Q235 steel.
Annealed Q235 steel will exhibit reduced mass change during high-temperature salt exposure relative to untreated Q235 steel.
Annealed Q235 steel will exhibit less pitting during high-temperature salt exposure relative to untreated Q235 steel.
Oxide-formation and oxide-evolution kinetics are slower at room temperature than at 700–900 °C.
Annealing will produce minimal differences in oxide characteristics and corrosion performance at room temperature relative to untreated Q235 steel.
The proposed protective mechanism applies under aggressive salt exposure at 700–900 °C but is unlikely to produce significant protection differences at room temperature.
